title: Niagara: A 32-Way Multithreaded SPARC Processor
decision: Optimized for throughput on commercial server workloads by exploiting thread-level parallelism (TLP) rather than chasing higher single-thread instruction-level parallelism (ILP).
alternatives_or_rejected: Rejected the prevailing approach of building more complex, deeply pipelined, out-of-order ILP processors. The paper argues that for commercial server code — which exhibits low ILP, high cache-miss rates, unpredictable branches, and frequent load-load dependencies — the performance advantage of a complex ILP processor over a simple single-issue processor is not significant, while the ILP processor incurs high power and complexity costs.
rationale: Commercial server applications have large degrees of client-request-level parallelism (TLP) but low ILP. Memory access time — not single-thread instruction throughput — limits performance. Therefore throughput must be increased by running many threads concurrently, not by speeding up one thread.
outcome: Defined the guiding philosophy for the entire Niagara design: aggregate many simple, multithreaded cores on a single die with a shared high-bandwidth memory subsystem, targeting performance/watt instead of single-thread speed.

title: Niagara: A 32-Way Multithreaded SPARC Processor
decision: Organize the chip as 8 thread groups ('SPARC pipes'), each group integrating 4 threads that share a single-issue, 6-stage in-order pipeline, yielding 32 hardware threads; switch between threads on a zero-cycle penalty to hide memory and pipeline stalls.
alternatives_or_rejected: The paper describes the multithreading design space (coarse-grain vertical multithreading, simultaneous multithreading, chip multiprocessing) and chose fine-grain vertical multithreading with 4 threads per pipe. This rejects SMT (which typically works on superscalar processors) and rejects giving each thread its own full pipeline. It also implies rejecting a small number of complex SMT cores in favor of many simple fine-grain-multithreaded cores.
rationale: Four threads per pipe is enough to hide the latency of long-latency operations (e.g., 3-cycle load latency) by switching to another thread every cycle, while keeping the shared pipeline simple and low-power. The paper states the hardware 'hides memory and pipeline stalls on a given thread by scheduling the other threads in the group onto the SPARC pipe with a zero cycle switch penalty,' and that 'reusing the shared processing pipeline results in higher throughput.'
outcome: 32 concurrently executing hardware threads; each SPARC pipe issues up to one instruction per cycle per active thread group, sustaining throughput even under high cache-miss rates.

title: Niagara: A 32-Way Multithreaded SPARC Processor
decision: Use a simple, single-issue, 6-stage (F, S, D, E, M, W) in-order SPARC pipeline with minimal speculation rather than a complex out-of-order, superscalar, deeply pipelined core.
alternatives_or_rejected: Rejected the complex-ILP-processor approach. The paper states that the performance advantage of a complex ILP processor over a single-issue processor is not significant for commercial server workloads, while the ILP processor incurs high power and complexity. The design therefore deliberately omits out-of-order execution and large instruction-window machinery.
rationale: Because commercial workloads are bound by memory latency (not by single-thread instruction throughput), a simple pipeline whose stalls are hidden by thread switching achieves comparable effective throughput at a fraction of the power and area. The paper frames this as 'a more efficient approach... to build a machine using simple cores aggregated on a single die.'
outcome: Simple cores enabled 8 cores to fit on a single die at 90nm, contributing directly to the chip's high throughput-per-watt. (Final silicon: 279M transistors, 378mm², 1.2GHz, ~63–72W.)
paper_vs_general: confident-this-is-in-the-paper for the simple-pipeline decision; power/area numbers are from-general-Niagara-knowledge-not-necessarily-this-paper

title: Niagara: A 32-Way Multithreaded SPARC Processor
decision: Pair small per-core private L1 caches (16KB I + 8KB D, 4-way set-associative) with a large shared 3MB L2 cache that is 4-way banked, pipelined, and 12-way set-associative; feed the L2 with four independent DDR2 memory controllers delivering >20GB/s.
alternatives_or_rejected: Rejected equipping each core with large private L1/L2 caches (the traditional ILP-processor approach). The paper notes the cache sizes 'are a good trade-off between miss rates, area, and the ability of other threads in the group to hide latency' — i.e., large private caches are unnecessary because thread switching hides miss latency, and die area is better spent on more threads and a shared L2.
rationale: Commercial server code has large working sets and data sharing; a shared on-chip L2 eliminates the high-latency coherent interconnect traffic that discrete-processor SMP systems suffer, replacing it with low-latency shared-cache communication. 12-way associativity minimizes conflict misses from the many threads; 4-way banking supplies the bandwidth. The crossbar provides >200GB/s bandwidth between cores and L2 banks.
outcome: 3MB shared L2 with 4×750KB independent banks, 2-cycle throughput / 8-cycle latency; >20GB/s to DRAM. The paper reports that on real commercial applications, performance scales almost linearly with the number of threads, demonstrating no bandwidth bottlenecks in the design.

title: Niagara: A 32-Way Multithreaded SPARC Processor
decision: Implement a simple cache coherence protocol: L1 caches are write-through with allocate-on-load and no-allocate-on-store; the L2 maintains a directory that shadows the L1 tags, tracking sharers at L1-line granularity.
alternatives_or_rejected: Rejected a conventional SMP-style coherence protocol over off-chip coherent interconnects. The paper notes that in conventional SMP systems using discrete processors, 'coherence misses go out over low-frequency off-chip buses or links, and can have high latencies.' The on-chip shared-L2 design allows a much simpler protocol.
rationale: Write-through L1 with a no-allocate store policy means only invalidation messages are required; data can always be retrieved from the L2, simplifying the protocol. The L2 directory shadows L1 tags so coherence is enforced among the 8 cores without off-chip traffic. This 'simple cache coherence protocol' matches the overall design goal of minimizing complexity and power.
outcome: A lightweight coherence mechanism that, combined with the shared L2, eliminates off-chip coherence misses and supports the 32-thread throughput goal with low overhead.
